Passage: Mr. Baratta, an associate in William Diamond Design, might not count himself among the handful of dedicated map collectors who pore over sea charts, town plans and early world views - serious collectors who carefully store their prized possessions in flat file cabinets. He is among a new breed for whom the geographic or historical interest of a map is secondary to esthetic appeal. These days more and more people are buying maps because they look good, fill walls and come at the right price.
''In the last 10 years there's been a revolution in the way Americans view maps,'' said Richard Lan, an antiquarian book and map dealer in New York City.
The increased interest in maps comes at a time when people seem to know less about geography, said Dorothy Globus, the curator of exhibitions at the Cooper-Hewitt Museum. She is organizing a show on old and new maps to open in 1992, commemorating the 500th anniversary of Columbus's first voyage to the Americas.
Mrs. Globus, whose name means globe in German and who collects globes, said her own passion for maps came from moving around as ''a Foreign Service brat'' and reading National Geographic.
Those who have graduated from National Geographic to antique maps are finding prices relatively affordable, at least in comparison to original Currier & Ives lithographs and Audubon engravings.
''There's really nothing else in that price category that gives you the impact on a wall that a map does,'' said Robert K. Lewis, a New York-based decorator who has a few early navigational charts in his own collection.
In the middle and low end of the market, the supply is plentiful. At Argosy, the busy East 59th Street book and print shop where customers help themselves to map files for every state and country, prices range from $25 to $5,000. Expect to pay about $40 for an 1862 map of New York State, or $1,500 for a 1588 world map with colorful flying fish and sea monsters plying the Atlantic.
The increased demand has driven up the cost of the most valuable maps. In 1985, a copy of Francesco Rosselli's 1508 world map sold at Sotheby's for $44,000, which Selby Kiffer, Sotheby's vice president for books and manuscripts, said is the most ever paid for a map.
Less rare but still very desirable is a 1630 world map by Willem Blaeu, bordered by town views and costumed natives. It ''is a gorgeous example from the golden age of map making,'' said Paul Cohen of Richard B. Arkway, New York City map dealers. The firm has priced the map at $6,500, up from $4,500 two years ago.
Prices, of course, depend not only on the age of a map, but also on condition, subject and how many prints were made. Dealers who specialize in maps, most of them members of the Antiquarian Booksellers Association of America, have proliferated in Manhattan.
Other maps are collected purely for visual appeal. Maps of islands, with their irregular shapes, are especially popular, Mr. Lan said. He has in stock a vividly colored 1660 map by the Dutch cartographer Peter Goos showing California as an island, as it was customarily depicted even into the 1700's.
Color maps are the most popular for decorative purposes, according to collectors and dealers. But black-and-white maps appeal to the decorator Chessy Rayner, a partner in the New York-based firm Mac II. ''I think black and white has a snappy, more tailored look,'' she said. Ms. Rayner takes the traditional approach that maps work best in libraries, dens and offices. ''I wouldn't use one in a formal dining room,'' she said.
Keith Irvine, of Irvine and Fleming, another Manhattan-based decorating firm, also likes black-and-white maps. ''They have the look of old steel engravings,'' he said. He once papered the walls of a sunroom with them.
Virtually all maps available today came from books and atlases and were meant to be examined closely.
William Diamond prefers large-scale maps that, as Mr. Baratta put it, can be read across a room. A few years ago he helped furnish a family room for Brenda Feldman on Long Island with two matched folding screens from the 1920's, depicting the hemispheres.
Recently, at a Massachusetts antiques show, Mr. Baratta and Mr. Diamond picked up a set of 1930's school maps, ''the kind you pull down on shades,'' Mr. Baratta said. Mr. Diamond plans to frame all 12 - and use them in his own apartment.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here are some productivity tools that may help you with your time management:

1. Trello: Trello is a project management tool that allows you to organize and prioritize your to-do lists and tasks using a visual "board" format. You can drag and drop items between different lists, label them with due dates and priorities, and collaborate with team members.

2. Asana: Asana is a similar project management tool that allows you to track tasks and projects, set deadlines, and communicate with team members. It has additional features like tracking progress, delegating tasks, and creating templates for recurring projects.

3. RescueTime: RescueTime is a time tracking tool that runs in the background on your computer or mobile device and automatically logs how much time you spend on different apps, websites, and tasks. You can set productivity goals and receive reports on how much time you're spending on different activities, which can help you adjust your habits.

4. Focus@Will: Focus@Will is a music app that uses neuroscience to help you stay focused and productive while you work. It offers a variety of instrumental music tracks that are scientifically optimized to help you concentrate and reduce distractions.

5. Forest: Forest is a productivity app that uses gamification to encourage you to stay focused on your tasks. You "plant a tree" in the app and it grows over time as long as you stay on task. If you leave the app to check social media or do something else, the tree withers and dies. Over time, you can collect virtual coins that you can use to plant real trees in partnership with tree-planting organizations.

These tools are just a few examples of the many resources available to help you improve your time management skills. Dana Gioia asked, “can poetry matter?” and the hesitant response from those concerned, calling from the last century to this one, was we certainly hope so.
This interview is the first entry in a new topic we are starting on Poems Out Loud that we are calling “Letter from a Young Poet” in which we will chronicle the experiences and insights of young poets as they find out what it means to call oneself a writer: from contests and rejections, to themes and obsessions, to what bids each of them to write.
Michael Rutherglen is from Charlottesville, Virginia. He was the recipient of a 2008 Ruth Lilly Fellowship from the Poetry Foundation. Some of his work has (quite magically) appeared in Poetry, The Colorado Review, and Prairie Schooner, and more is forthcoming in the Antioch Review. He lives in San Francisco.
Poems Out Loud: What is your day job?
Rutherglen: I work as a graphic designer at a small book design company in Oakland. As this occupies most of the daylit hours of the week and is but obliquely related to my true interest in life, I would have to call it simply a day job.
Poems Out Loud: How do you believe having your first book published will change your life?
Rutherglen: I think it will be comforting to pose my own slender volume against all the titles constantly eyeing me from my shelves. In particular, I am looking forward to an endless staring content between my author photo and the spine of James Merrill’s Collected Poems.
Poems Out Loud: Who do you read?
Rutherglen: Shakespeare is the foundation of my reading: every Sunday, I read one of the plays. After him, I’ve been rereading the Romantic poets, alongside Donne, Herbert, Hopkins, and Yeats of late. As for contemporary writers, Jorie Graham, Jack Gilbert, Seamus Heaney, A. R. Ammons, Lucie Brock-Broido, and Richard Kenney are in fairly steady rotation. In prose, Nabokov has been my latest project.
Poems Out Loud: How did you come to write poetry?
Rutherglen: To amend an old Zen punchline, it’s women all the way down: first my mother, an English professor, who read Dante to me when I was a kid, and then Mrs. Staggers, my third grade teacher, who organized an intensive unit on poetry that year. Later, Lisa Russ Spaar, my undergraduate advisor, was instrumental in directing me towards writing seriously.
Poems Out Loud: How often do you write?
Rutherglen: Every morning and some afternoons.
Poems Out Loud: What do you give up or sacrifice in order to write?
Poems Out Loud: What is the best advice you’ve received?
Poems Out Loud: Do many of your friends read or write poetry?
Rutherglen: Among those who are not writers, a few read poetry seriously.

Rutherglen: I recently moved to San Francisco, where I am sure there are several such communities. Anchorite that I am, I have yet to feel my way into any of them.

Rutherglen: The dream of a teaching job has long hovered vaguely in the middle distance, but I’m focused on the foreground these days, on writing my first book.

Historical Relationship Between Art and Mental Illness

The relationship between art and mental illness has not changed much since the days of Van Gogh and Munch. The link between creativity and mental illness has been an ongoing debate for many years. Many people believe that there is a correlation between the two, while others are not sure. Art therapy has been shown to be an effective treatment for a variety of mental health problems, including depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (American Art Therapy Association, n.d.). The benefits of art therapy include improving self-esteem, reducing stress and anxiety, and increasing self-awareness.

The American Art Therapy Association promotes the importance of art therapy as a treatment for mental illness, and many universities now offer degrees in art therapy.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Art therapy has proven to be an effective treatment for people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD is a mental health condition that can occur after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event, such as a natural disaster, physical assault, or military combat. Symptoms of PTSD may include flashbacks, nightmares, anxiety, and depression.

Art therapy can be used to address the emotional and physical symptoms of PTSD and help individuals process and work through their trauma. One common technique used in art therapy for PTSD is gradual exposure, where the patient creates a series of images or crafts that gradually represent the traumatic event, leading up to a final piece that represents a place of safety or healing.

Another technique used in art therapy for PTSD is called grounding. Grounding techniques aim to help the individual stay present and focused in the moment, rather than being triggered by past trauma. This often involves using sensory-based activities, such as painting, drawing, or sculpture.

Art therapy can also be used in group settings or as part of a larger treatment plan that includes other therapies, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy or medication. Additionally, art therapy can be customized to the individual's needs and preferences, making it a flexible and adaptive form of therapy.

Overall, art therapy provides a safe and supportive space for individuals with PTSD to express and process their feelings related to trauma.
